articles.headline: Treasury Designates Eight Digital Asset Service Providers for Iran Sanctions Evasion
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations, targeting eight digital asset service providers. These entities are accused of assisting the Iranian regime in evading sanctions and funding terrorism by exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets.

According to OFAC, several of these businesses have sent funds to digital asset accounts linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and other terrorist activities. Many also reportedly dealt with Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges that had already been sanctioned by the United States. Some of the designated firms attempted to avoid detection by changing their names and addresses, but continued operations despite public warnings about the risks they posed.

This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' an ongoing effort by the United States to cut off revenue streams that the Iranian regime uses to finance terrorism, weapons proliferation, and its proxies throughout the Middle East. The U.S. coordinated this action with Canada, including FINTRAC, Canada's financial intelligence unit, reflecting a shared commitment to protecting the North American financial system from abuse.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Cuban Entities and Individuals, Targets Key Economic Sectors
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations designations, alongside Cuba designations and the publication of a Cuba-related determination. These actions target eight entities and two individuals linked to Cuba's financial, shipping, and military procurement networks.

The sanctions aim to counter the Cuban government's alleged activities that pose a threat to U.S. national security, specifically targeting individuals and organizations involved in the Cuban regime's oil shipping operations, state-owned import and technical-support companies, and Chinese suppliers of military equipment.

Furthermore, the U.S. issued a determination that paves the way for future sanctions on the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy. This expansion of sanctions under Executive Order 14404 signifies a broader effort to restrict the Cuban regime's ability to funnel resources to its military elite and profit from opaque offshore networks.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. Concurrently, OFAC published an Iran-related alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a related Frequently Asked Question.

The Iran-related actions are part of ongoing efforts to address the Iranian regime's illicit activities. The accompanying OFAC Alert specifically highlights the Iranian 'shadow fleet's' reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion, underscoring the risks for maritime stakeholders.

Regarding Venezuela, OFAC issued an amended General License 5Y, which authorizes certain transactions related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 Percent Bond on or after September 17, 2026. Additionally, an amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 595, was issued to provide further clarity on these authorized transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License FF-1 for Wind Down of Transactions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Iran General License FF-1, titled 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.' This amended general license provides a specific authorization for the winding down of certain transactions.

General License FF-1 is a crucial instrument for entities needing to divest from or cease operations with the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance in a compliant manner. It outlines the scope of authorized activities during the wind-down period.

This action follows previous Iran-related general licenses and designations, reflecting OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions implementation and its commitment to providing clear guidance for compliance.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities for North Korea and DRC Sanctions Evasion
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions target individuals and entities involved in facilitating illicit activities for both regimes.

The North Korea-related designations include Russian and North Korean nationals linked to entities such as LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY ALIS, CHINYONG INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY COOPERATION COMPANY, and FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER. These individuals and entities are accused of supporting DPRK IT worker fraud targeting U.S. businesses.

The DRC-related designations include Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society (Zigama CSS), a Kigali-based financial institution. These designations are in response to Rwanda's alleged destabilizing activities in Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, particularly in support of the M23 group.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider. Extreme Networks has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to resolve its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and related services from the United States to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was majority-owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, a designated Russian state-owned defense company, making MMZA a blocked person by operation of law.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement emphasizes the critical importance of conducting thorough sanctions-related diligence before acquiring a company or its assets, maintaining vigilance regarding sanctions risks, and ensuring adequate oversight of foreign activities and operations.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update is part of OFAC's ongoing process to review and ensure its published guidance remains current.

The amendments cover 11 specific FAQs (10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53) and address key areas such as which jurisdictions are subject to broad sanctions, how to block an account or funds transfer, the interest required on blocked funds, and when to reject rather than block a transaction.

The updated guidance also clarifies notification procedures for customers when property is blocked, rules for account openings and transactions involving blocked persons, and the timing and procedures for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions. These revisions aim to provide clearer instructions for financial institutions and other U.S. persons to ensure compliance with sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran and Russia General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain Belarus and North Korea designations. Additionally, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.

The issuance of new General Licenses for Iran and Russia aims to authorize specific activities that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions programs. These licenses provide clarity and pathways for certain transactions, reflecting a nuanced approach to sanctions implementation.

The removal of some Belarus and North Korea designations indicates a recalibration of sanctions against these countries. These changes, along with the amended FAQs, are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to ensure its sanctions programs are effective and responsive to evolving geopolitical landscapes.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Chinese Entities Under PAIPA, Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, 'Transactions Authorized Pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations,' and PAIPA General License 2, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving Certain Entities Blocked on October 19, 2026.'

Several Chinese entities have been added to OFAC's Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List as a result of these actions. These include BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE I VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP (a.k.a. MIRACLE PLUS RMB FUND I), BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE II VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP (a.k.a. MIRACLE PLUS RMB FUND II), and BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN ZHIYUAN ENTERPRISE MANAGEMENT CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP.

The designations impose various restrictions, including the blocking of all property and interests in property of these entities, prohibitions on transactions, and limitations on loans and credits from U.S. financial institutions. General License 2 specifically provides a limited authorization for the wind-down of transactions involving the newly blocked entities.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ for Earthquake Relief
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is issuing Venezuela-related General License 60A, 'Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela.' This new general license aims to facilitate humanitarian aid and recovery efforts in the region.

In addition to General License 60A, OFAC is also issuing one amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 1263. This amendment provides further clarification and guidance regarding the scope and application of the new general license, ensuring that humanitarian efforts can proceed without undue sanctions-related impediments.

This action underscores OFAC's commitment to allowing humanitarian assistance to reach those in need, even within sanctioned jurisdictions, by providing specific authorizations for such critical activities.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Fined $1.5 Million by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based artificial intelligence and cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations stemmed from Extreme Networks' export of networking equipment and related services to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer, between September 2018 and March 2022. MMZA was majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company, rendering it a blocked entity.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, leading to the significant penalty. This case highlights the importance of robust sanctions compliance programs, particularly in due diligence during acquisitions and oversight of foreign operations.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined Over $11 Million by OFAC for Sanctions Breaches

This enforcement action underscores OFAC's continued vigilance in ensuring that financial institutions adhere strictly to U.S. sanctions regulations across all their operations and client interactions.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors, Transfers from USML to EAR
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the Department of State's U.S. Munitions List (USML).

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with the controls already applied to firearms. Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons.

License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors. Jeffrey I. Kessler, Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, stated that this move alleviates compliance burdens on the firearms industry while continuing to protect national security.

articles.headline: BIS Closes Semiconductor Export Control Loophole for Foreign Fabs in China
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has closed a loophole that previously allowed a handful of foreign companies to export semiconductor manufacturing equipment and technology to China without a license. This action aims to level the playing field by requiring these companies to obtain licenses, similar to their competitors.

This move by BIS is designed to strengthen U.S. export controls and prevent advanced semiconductor technology from being used to undermine American national security and foreign policy interests. The loophole had been a point of concern for policymakers seeking to restrict China's access to critical technologies.

The new requirement means that foreign-owned semiconductor fabrication plants operating in China will now face the same licensing requirements as U.S. companies when exporting certain equipment and technology. This is expected to increase compliance obligations for affected firms and further restrict China's ability to develop its advanced semiconductor industry.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

body: One child and one young adult were killed in the crash, local authorities say, with more injured.

articles.headline: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
body: No link has been established between the threats against the airlines and those against the media outlets.

articles.headline: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
body: Paul Mackenzie ordered his followers to starve their children to death in a forest so they could "meet Jesus".

articles.headline: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
body: Prosecutors begin investigating EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people.

articles.headline: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approval
body: The Trump administration had hoped the construction of the 250-foot arch could begin as early as this week.

articles.headline: Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
body: Pope Leo, who had part of a lung removed last month, will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

articles.headline: Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide
body: Jim Messina tells the BBC that after Democrats' midterm victories he's talked to "over two dozen campaigns", with some already hiring staff.

articles.headline: Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
body: The 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, says the charges are politically motivated.

articles.headline: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
body: Musk said it was to make room for production of its Cybercabs - autonomous taxis without a driver.

articles.headline: Somalia's top court rejects president's term extension amid political crisis
body: The country's first nationwide elections since 1969 are due next year - a timetable now thrown into doubt.

articles.headline: California governor commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
body: California has historically had the largest population of people on death row in the US.

articles.headline: Nigerian court rules opposition candidate cannot stand in elections
body: The high court has sacked the leadership of the opposition ADC party with only months to go until elections.

articles.headline: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
body: Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state".

articles.headline: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse
body: The move follows a bank collapse and after the lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial against him.

articles.headline: Watch: Is it the end of the road for Tesla's Cybertruck?
body: The car company's CEO Elon Musk has said production will halt in Texas, to focus on the firm's self-driving Cybercabs.

articles.headline: Bomb hoaxes: Messages reveal how threat was passed on by air traffic control
body: BBC Verify has been analysing messages after flights across Europe were targeted by fake bomb threats - the second such incident this week.

articles.headline: Was an Italian chef really fired over refusal to put pineapple on pizza?
body: The chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".

articles.headline: US midterm results spark fears in Israel over future of two countries' ties
body: Staunch US support of Israel has been raised as one of the reasons why Republicans performed so badly.
